bundleName: data publication brine blood and bilgewater.json

name: Name
body: Admiral Thorga Boomhowler raised her spyglass and peered over the calm, blue waters of the Meredius. "One ship, Hargor. What do you make of that?" First Mate Hargor Stormjaw rested his hands on the hilts of his twin cutlasses and chewed his ever-present cigar. "Sound like easy pickin’s to me." Boomhowler continued to study the lone ship. "Well, she’s low in the water, which means she’s full of loot—or sinking. Probably the latter. Looks like she’s seen a bit of rough treatment. Huh, there’s a menofix on her sail." "Bloody human gods," Hargor said and spat. "Not a one of ’em worth a pyg’s promise." Boomhowler slapped her first mate’s shoulder. "Hah! You sound like someone who has never had the distinct pleasure of fighting a ship full of fire-spewing zealots." "Maybe so, but the crew ain’t had any sport in weeks," Hargor said. "They’re gettin’ antsy, you know." Boomhowler glanced back at the crew, a motley assemblage of trollkin, pygs, and towering reef trolls lined up along the gunwales of The Baying Wolf, her thirty-two-gun frigate, and snorted. "You mean they haven’t been paid in an age."

name: Name
body: "Or killed no one neither," Hargor said. "Been two weeks since we plucked that Ordic frigate. A ripe fruit, that one was." "Ripe and deadly. You must remember you lost an arm there." "Aye, but it grew back," Hargor flexed his left bicep. "Madrak was mighty pleased with the bounty it yielded, if you remember." Her first mate was right. It had been too long since they’d last taken a ship. The Orgoth incursion had disrupted the shipping lanes to the point that the stretch between Zu and western Immoren had all but emptied of vessels, and those they did find were often heavily armed or guarded. The Southern Kriels and their leader, Madrak Ironside, depended on Boomhowler’s ships to provide them with supplies to feed thousands of hungry trollkin and gold to purchase weapons, bribe officials, and, more importantly, build more ships. It was that last bit that made up her mind. She grinned. "All right, I’m convinced. We’ll take her." Hargor rubbed his blunt-fingered hands together. "Excellent. What’ll it be, Admiral? Death from above again?"

name: Name
body: The Baying Wolf carried half a dozen pyg-piloted airships that could drop bombs on enemy vessels, but they were running short on munitions. Boomhowler shook her head. "Those little blighters are a mite too liberal with the few bombs we have left." "Death from below then?" Hargor said. "Hullripper and Plankeater ain’t been fed in a bit. I’m sure they wouldn’t mind a bite of Menite." The two deepborn dire trolls aboard The Baying Wolf were nightmares of scales, fins, and fangs. Always hungry, they could chew through an enemy ship’s hull and send it to the bottom in minutes. They were hard to control, even with Boomhowler’s warlock abilities, and even more so once their blood was up. She shook her head. "It’s a challenge to loot a ship under a dozen leagues of water, and being honest, I might like to take a prisoner or two." Then she turned to address the crew. "I’m told you bunch of degenerate barnacle biters ache for a spot of exercise." Her fellcaller’s voice thundering across the ship. "Is that right?"

name: Name
body: "Aye, Admiral!" came the enthusiastic response. Boomhowler turned back to Hargor. "If you’d be so kind as to prepare the boarding parties, I’ll lead them." Her first mate grinned over his cigar. "Aye, Admiral. Death from everywhere it is." *** The Menite ship was a single-masted cog armed with four cannons at port and starboard. They opened up on The Baying Wolf as she closed in, but half their shots sailed over the deck, and the two that struck bounced off the frigate’s reinforced hull. Then they were alongside, the boarding planks dropped, and the world dissolved into the red mist of combat. Boomhowler was first over the gunwales, her two reef trolls, Gulper and Gasher, close behind, and her amphibious familiar, Slim, coiled around her hat, tentacles waving menacingly. As soon as her feet thumped down on the enemy ship’s deck, half a dozen human warriors clad in archaic armor and wielding flaming spears charged her. She parried a spear with Black Heart, her cutlass, and ran through the man behind it. Slim flailed his tentacles at the soldier next to the man Boomhowler had just killed. The Menite recoiled for an instant, his spearpoint dipping, and Boomhowler shot him in the guts with her hand cannon before he could recover.

name: Name
body: Gulper and Gasher charged past her, singing drunken shanties in deep burbling troll-speak. Both carried enormous casks of rum strapped to their backs and had partaken liberally before the attack—reef trolls fought better when they were soused. Gasher hacked a spearman in half with his oversized cutlass, and Gulper, true to his name, bit the head clean off another and swallowed it whole. Their emotions surged through Boomhowler’s connection with them, a heady mixture of boundless rage and wild joy. More Menite soldiers surged up from the hold, though these had a more ragtag look than the spearmen who’d met her initial charge. They were armed with a motley collection of hand weapons and their piecemeal armor bore menofixes hastily scrawled with red paint on breastplates or pauldrons. The thundering cry of The Baying Wolf’s crew filled the air as they swarmed over the boarding planks. They paused for a single breath to fire pistols into the massed defenders, then they charged into the melee with cutlasses and boarding axes.

name: Name
body: Boomhowler cut down another spearman and found herself in a lull from the combat. She took this opportunity to summon her magic. The defenders of the Menite ship were not well equipped, but they fought with a zealot’s abandon, and she’d lose no more of her crew than absolutely necessary to the conflict. Power rolled through her then burst forth in a wave of azure brilliance. The Dhunian blessing bolstered the trollkin’s natural resilience and regenerative capabilities for a short time, and she saw, to her relief, three mortally wounded crewmen get up off the deck and rejoin the fight.

name: Name
body:
After that, the fight became more massacre than anything resembling a real battle, and human bodies soon littered the deck. The Menites fought on, however, and Boomhowler came to the not-unwelcome realization she’d have to kill every one of them. She raised Black Heart to strike down another spearman but faltered when a loud clear voice rang out over the melee.
"In the name of Menoth, stop!"
The power in that voice was something even a fellcaller could appreciate, and all eyes turned to the opening that led down into the hold. Boomhowler expected to see a towering human warrior, perhaps one of the potent Menite knights that had come within an eyelash of killing her when last she’d encountered the human zealots. Instead, she saw a stooped old man, his long hair and beard as silver as a pale moon. He wore white robes adorned with menofixes picked out in gold, and he carried a long staff topped with the cross-shaped sigil of his god.
"Who leads here?" The priest asked.
Boomhowler considered just getting on with the slaughter, but there was a strength to the priest that intrigued her.

name: Name
body:
"Parley!" she called out, and each of her crew took a grudging step away from the Menite they were about to kill. She then addressed the priest. "I’m Admiral Thorga Boomhowler of the Southern Kriels, and this is my crew."
The Menite priest walked slowly across the blood-soaked deck, the bottom of his robe quickly turning pink in the gore. He stopped before Boomhowler and stared at her, his blue eyes cold and appraising. "I am Creedan Versh, a priest of Menoth. Why have you attacked our ship?"
"These waters are claimed by the Southern Kriels," Boomhowler said. "All ships and their valuables belong to us."
"Valuables? We do not carry gold or jewels, Admiral Boomhowler, only mercy."
Boomhowler frowned. "Mercy?"
"Let me show you."
***
The hold was dark and cool and filled with crates, barrels, and sealed boxes. Versh pointed his staff at the collected goods. "Inspect them as you will."
Boomhowler indicated five crewmen, including Hargor, and they went about opening the containers. After ten minutes, they returned to her side, looks of profound disappointment on their faces.

name: Name
body: "Food and medical supplies," Hargor said. "Not even junk jewelry in the whole lot." "These goods are bound for Immoren. Unique healing reagents from Zu to treat burns inflicted by Orgoth weapons and food to feed those displaced by their incursions," Versh said. The Baying Wolf had encountered and avoided the dreaded Orgoth warships northwest of Alchiere, but Boomhowler had attacked some of their smaller vessels. She shuddered at the memory of the Orgoth holds, which more resembled abattoirs than any place sane and rational beings would store their goods. "It ain’t much, but we could still use it," Hargor said. Boomhowler sheathed her cutlass and sighed. The fight was draining out of her, and something else was left in its wake. Compassion was a right pain in the arse for a pirate captain. "All right, priest, I need you to surrender to me." "My soldiers are dead. The ship is yours. What more is there to surrender?" Versh said. "I know, but I need you to say it." Versh shook his head but complied. "Very well. We surrender."

name: Name
body: A collective groan went up from the trollkin crewmembers in the hold. The Baying Wolf operated under a strict charter, and one of the tenets of that charter was that enemy crewmembers who asked for quarter would be granted it. "Shut your gobs, you bunch of wet-arsed whelps," Boomhowler shouted. "You know the rules." "What are your orders, then, Admiral?" Hargor asked. "Gather weapons and armor from the slain and take half the food in the hold. Leave the medical supplies." Hargor nodded and went to carry out her orders. Versh suddenly said, "Thousands will die if you take that food." Boomhowler ignored the dire prediction and stepped close to Versh, looming over the stooped priest. "You know, priest, there are trollkin in western Immoren suffering as much as any humans. Tell me true: will any of these supplies reach them?" The priest Versh looked Boomhowler in the eyes, something few had the nerve to do. "Mercy is not solely a human trait, Admiral, nor do only humans deserve it." Boomhowler nodded. "You said thousands would die if we took these goods, but how many more will die if you don’t reach western Immoren at all? Your ship is a wreck. You’ll be smashed to bits by storms or rough water, of which you’ll find plenty up north. We’ll patch you up, and you can consider what we take as fair work for fair pay."

name: Name
body: A brief smile flashed across the old priest’s face, one that might have once been hidden by a mask. "You are merciful, Admiral." "Dhunia’s breath," Boomhowler muttered. "Promise me you won’t spread that around."

name: Name
title: Part 2:\nThe Enemy of My Enemy Is an Opportunity

name: Name
body: Captain Badloche Firequill stood over a collection of charts spread across a table in his quarters. On the top of the pile was a large map of western Immoren that included the Alchiere subcontinent. Firequill leaned over and traced his recent path north with one finger. He’d taken his war galley The Archon’s Lament and a handful of smaller ships from the Brineblood fleet from the Sea of Alchiere, past Ancient Icthier, to within fifty nautical miles of the Bay of Cygnar. It was dangerous, possibly reckless, but with the Orgoth prowling the seas, prey was becoming scarce closer to home. He'd hidden in the shallows around the Mercarian Keys with hopes of waylaying a fat trading vessel out of Mercir. With the Cygnarans fighting the Orgoth, traders couldn’t count on protective escorts, and that made them easy prey. Of course, if the Cygnaran Navy caught wind of pirates operating in their waters, they’d almost certainly divert a warship or two to deal with it, but it was worth the risk.

name: Name
body: The thunder of cannon fire from above suddenly rocked Firequill’s cabin, nearly sending him sprawling. Seconds later, his cabin door flew open, and his bosun, the hulking Gibber Stonesurf, burst in. At over seven feet tall, she could nearly match a reef troll for sheer strength and meanness. "Cap’n," Gibber said. "Got us a situation topside." Firequill grabbed his brace of pistols and slung them over his shoulder. His giant starfish familiar, Ringo, sensing danger, climbed out of his tank near Firequill’s bed, scuttled across the floor, and climbed up onto his master’s shoulder. "Are we shooting or being shot at, Bosun?" "Uh, neither," Gibber said and regarded Ringo with a wary frown. The starfish had a bad habit of snatching "souvenirs" from crewmembers who wandered too close. "Well, we can’t have that now, can we?" Firequill said. "Lead the way." *** The crew had gathered on the starboard gunwales of the The Archon’s Lament,, where nearly a hundred trollkin and pygs were cheering and loudly placing bets.

name: Name
body: "Captain on deck!" Gibber bellowed, her voice a tsunami of sound, and the crew parted immediately to let Firequill through. Nine hundred yards from The Archon’s Lament’s position, a pair of warships were engaged in a pitched battle. The first was a Cygnaran frigate, sputtering blue sparks through a gaping hole in its side where a cannon ball had smashed through and damaged its galvanic engine. Its guns unloaded cannon fire and gouts of lightning onto their enemy, a ship the sight of which gave even Firequill pause. The Orgoth warship was a massive, ungainly thing fitted with a pair of steam-powered paddlewheels to drive it through the water. Its jet-black hull bristled with cannons, while its deck swarmed with horrors beneath sails the color of freshly spilled blood. Both ships had taken a beating, but the Cygnaran vessel had received the worst of it. The Orgoth ship was bigger, better armed, and its captain had clearly surprised his foe and battered it with unanswered broadsides.

name: Name
body: "They see us yet?" Firequill asked. "Nah," Gibber replied. "You chose a good spot, Cap’n." Firequill had positioned his tiny fleet behind one of the hundreds of small islets in the Mercarian Keys, just south of Raelthorne Island. His galley and the four cogs with him had a good view of ships passing by but were shielded from detection themselves. "Two ships full of humans," Firequill said and drummed his fingers on the rail. "Probably should just let them slaughter each other." "Probably," Gibber said, eying Firequill warily. "But you’re not gonna, right?" "As much as I hate to admit it, one of yonder ships is worse than the other," Firequill said. "Which one?" Firequill snorted. "Well, one is full of blue-bellied, trollkin-murdering bastards and the other is Orgoth." *** By the time the Orgoth spotted The Archon’s Lament, Firequill was on top of them. The Orgoth vessel had just fired its cannons at the Cygnaran ship, and though they were certainly trying to reload their guns as fast as possible, Firequill had chosen his moment perfectly.

name: Name
body: "Fire!" he bellowed, and all twenty heavy cannons on the starboard side opened up with a stuttering roar. He’d ordered chain shot loaded into the guns, and a dozen Orgoth sailors were reduced to gory chunks as the cannon-propelled chains slashed into them. The shot hit both paddlewheels on the enemy vessel as well, reducing them to shreds of wood and metal and leaving the ship dead in the water. Their first attack had crippled the Orgoth ship, but Firequill was far from done. Pyg-piloted airships aboard his smaller cogs had launched and now floated overhead. The sharp whine of descending bombs filled the air, and the blood-swamped deck of the Orgoth ship bloomed red and yellow with incendiary bursts, setting the decks and what remained of the paddlewheels alight. The Archon’s Lament pulled alongside the Orgoth ship, but Firequill eschewed boarding action for a more favored tactic. He drew his magelock pistol and scattergun and made contact with the minds of the three reef trolls on board, each armed with a ship’s gun. He sent the trolls to the gunwales, pointed his pistols at the decks of the Orgoth ship, and called out, "Shooting gallery, lads! Let ’em have it!"

name: Name
body: Trollkin armed with heavy pistols and pyg deck-cannon crews fired their weapons, smashing holes in the Orgoth ship and cutting down enemy sailors who ventured onto the deck to fight or to douse the flames. The reef trolls fired their ship guns, and seconds later, Gibber, on the battery deck below, blasted another broadside into the Orgoth ship’s hull. Firequill aimed and fired his magelocks, taking down a pair of Orgoth warriors who’d somehow survived the first salvo. One of them was only wounded, however, and he managed to aim and fire his own weapon. The heavy projectile whizzed past Firequill’s head, singeing his beard quills, and causing him to duck. Ringo, still perched on his shoulder, snatched one of Firequill’s spare hand cannons and fired it. The shot was true, and the Orgoth warrior sagged to the flaming deck. "Nice shot, Ringo," Firequill said and patted his familiar. The starfish twirled the hand cannon in a flashy spin then returned it to its hook on Firequill’s bandolier. The Cygnaran vessel, realizing they weren’t actually facing two enemies, rejoined the battle and unleashed a fusillade of their own into the Orgoth ship. Caught between The Archon’s Lament and their original target, the hull of the black warship buckled and cracked beneath a concentrated barrage of cannon fire and gouts of voltaic energy. The Orgoth vessel listed to the side and then slipped beneath the waves, leaving a crimson stain on the water and dozens of floating corpses.

name: Name
body: The battle over, Gibber came up from the battery deck to stand beside Firequill. The Cygnaran ship was a hundred yards away, its crew staring across the water at their saviors. "What’ll we do about them?" Gibber asked. "Send word to their captain," Firequill said. "Tell him I’d like to drink to our victory aboard The Archon’s Lament. Now." Gibber chuckled. "I’ll break out the good rum." *** Captain Banner Turlough of Morrow’s Mercy was tall and lean with a narrow, wolfish face and a shock of iron-grey hair tied in a mussed queue. His armor—breastplate and pauldrons—was dented, scorched, and blood splattered, and both the cutlass and hand cannon at his side had seen very recent use. Firequill approved. A captain who didn’t fight beside his crew had no right to that rank or title. The Cygnaran stood before the chart table in Firequill’s cabin, holding a tumbler of good rum. "Thank you for your assistance, Captain Firequill." "I’ve no love for Cygnar, but the Orgoth are a plague on every man or troll with salt and sea in his veins," Firequill said and tossed back his rum. "It’s Dhunia’s own work to send those bastards to the bottom."

name: Name
body: "On that we are agreed," Turlough said and finished his own drink. He stared at Firequill, and the tension in the room grew like the stench of bilgewater after a long voyage. Firequill was content to let the Cygnaran stew in it. Finally, Turlough cleared his throat and said, "I appreciate the drink, Captain, but something tells me this isn’t a social call." "Astute," Firequill replied. "I asked you here to discuss the terms of your surrender." Turlough shook his head. "I suppose it was foolish of me to think a pirate’s assistance came without a price." Firequill shrugged. "As you say, Captain." "And if I refuse to surrender?" "Then I’ll cripple your ship, board it, feed half your crew to my trolls, take everything I can carry, and send youto the bottom of the Meredius as well." To his credit, Captain Turlough did not blanch or falter, and he held Firequill’s gaze. "I’ll be honest, surrendering my ship to pirates is a hell of a lot better than what the Orgoth had in store for us." "I won’t argue with that," Firequill said and poured himself and Turlough another tot of rum. "If you let us aboard without a tussle to take what we want, I promise to leave your crew and ship intact. Then we can part as friends."

name: Name
body: Turlough stared at the rum in his tumbler, a dark smirk on his face. "Well, friend, will you allow me to make you an offer?" Firequill waved his tumbler at the Cygnaran, intrigued. "Go ahead." "The skill and bravery of the Southern Kriels’ fleet is well known," Turlough said. "You’ve amply proven both today." Firequill rolled his eyes. "I’m not pretty enough to appreciate flattery, Captain Turlough." Turlough leaned forward, his eyes bright, passionate. "Then let me put it this way. The Orgoth are a scourge on humans and trollkin alike, wouldn’t you agree?" "I would." "Then why not fight with us?" Turlough said. "If we defeat them at sea, we cripple them on land. We could drive them from our shores. Together." Firequill sat back in his chair. "Trollkin have fought beside humans before. It didn’t work out well for us." "I know this, and I offer no excuses for what’s happened between our peoples," Turlough said. "But this is not a petty squabble between nations. This is an existential threat as dire as the Infernal War."

name: Name
body: "I don’t disagree. It is different, mostly because you need us more than we need you at the moment." "At the moment," Turlough said, then drew in a deep breath and continued. "You came to our aid today when you could have let the Orgoth sink us and then picked them off afterward. That tells me you’re more honorable than most pirates. That tells me you’re someone I’d be proud to fight beside." This time, there was no attempt at flattery. Turlough meant every word. It moved Firequill. "I don’t generally like humans, and I have good reasons for that, but I could see myself fighting beside a man like you. All that said, though, I may be more honorable than most, I’m still a pirate, and I don’t work for free." "The crown would pay you handsomely if you joined us," Turlough said. "Aye, they might, and that’s a discussion for another time. However, in the spirit of possible future cooperation, let’s call what I take off your ship today a down payment. A good faith deposit, if you like."

name: Name
body:
Captain Turlough nodded and offered his hand, an unexpected bit of courtesy. Firequill stood and gripped the Cygnaran’s wrist. "Until we meet again, Captain."
Turlough smiled. "Until then."

name: Name
body: From the personal journal of Berlag Goodhammer, ship’s surgeon, The Tenebrous Donard 3rd, Tempen 622 A.R. They brought a pyg gunner’s mate into surgery this morning. Poor little mite was stone-dead before I could even examine him. No wounds. No obvious cause of death, but the crewmembers that found him said they heard him whispering in his rack last night. Talking to someone and speaking in fearful tones. When I was at Fort Falk as a physician’s assistant, I saw men and trollkin paralyzed with fear. The pyg they brought in this morning? I’d say he died of it. Donard 5th More crew members complain of hearing voices and seeing fell things in the night. They drink too much, sleep too little, and exhaustion is taking a toll. I brought my concerns to first mate Bloodbite, and he said he’d tell the captain. I wanted a damn-sight more than that. I wanted to speak to Shadowtongue myself. It took some convincing, but Bloodbite got me an audience. I’d never been in the captain’s quarters before. It was cold and dark and the walls were hung with bundles of dried herbs that gave off a sickly-sweet smell. The captain was gaunt, pale even, and his scylla familiar perched on his shoulder like some rotting specter. He sat behind a table where a sea bird of some kind had been splayed and gutted. The entrails had been arranged in a precise manner next to the poor creature.

name: Name
body: "I understand you believe the shades aboard The Tenebrous are proving deleterious to the crew’s morale," the captain said to me. His voice was half-whisper, half-croak, and it made all the spit dry up in my mouth. "Begging your pardon, Captain, but I am," I said back. "We got one dead already, more scared witless, and even the bloody dire trolls in the hold cower and flinch at anything so loud as a mouse fart." "Your concern is not unfounded, but The Tenebrous exacts a heavy toll on her crew, living and dead," Shadowtongue said. That flummoxed and frightened me. "I don’t understand, Captain. What toll is that?" "This ship is a predator. The hungrier it gets, the more dangerous it grows. It must be fed." Shadowtongue pointed one long finger at the slaughtered bird on his table. "Worry not—I have just learned there is suitable prey in our path." I stood there not knowing what to say. What can you say in the face of such riddling madness? The captain mercifully dismissed me with a wave of his hand, and I left with my guts knotted in fear and my mind full of questions I wasn’t sure I wanted answered.

name: Name
body: Donard 7th The Tenebrous sails north. We passed through the Mercarian Keys, skirted Cullenrock Island, and now drift up the Broken Coast. Too bloody close to Cygnar and Cryx, you ask me, but Captain Shadowtongue seems unconcerned. The winds are unreliable, but when we find ourselves becalmed for too long, Shadowtongue appears on deck, and a gale suddenly springs up, fills our sails, and pushes us farther north. It feels like we’re waiting for something, but none of us knows what. We’ve seen no other ships, but Captain Shadowtongue spends more and more time on deck, looking out over the misty waters as if he’s searching for something. I hope he doesn’t find it. Donard 8th This morning, the lookout spotted a ship on the horizon. Both hull and sails were a fearful ebony, visible even through the fog. A Cryxian blackship. Captain Shadowtongue ordered us to pursue. "The dark skeins of fate have put us in the path of that ship," Shadowtongue called out to the crew. "The dead cry out for vengeance as our hold cries out for ill-gotten lucre."

name: Name
body: He clenched his hands into fists, and queer green flames sprung around them. "I will deliver both!" The crew liked that and cheered their captain, though I doubt less than half of them know what in hell lucre is. Still, I was glad to see them in good spirits after these past dark, troubling days. "Prepare yourselves. Death awaits us." Shadowtongue grinned, a rare and, I must admit, terrifying sight. "And no one pays better." Donard 9th I’ll give Shadowtongue his due: he’s a crafty buccaneer. We crept up on the blackship, using the fog for cover, our sails filled with the unnatural wind. We took our battle stations, and I joined the crew on deck, my surgeon’s kit at my side, my best cleaver in hand. The Tenebrous opened up with a starboard battery, smashing into the Cryxian vessel with thunderous fury. Any other ship would have been blown to pieces beneath that assault, but the blackship hardly seemed damaged, and when she returned fire, my work began. Chain and grapeshot ripped into us, swamping us in gore as trollkin and pygs were torn asunder. I helped those I could—tying off arteries, pulling shot and shrapnel from wounded trollkin so they could regenerate proper. We lost half a dozen in that first barrage, but it was far from over.

name: Name
body: Our reef trolls and that great, horrible squid-headed thing we keep in the deepest part of the hold surged onto the deck at Shadowtongue’s command. Bloodbite piloted The Tenebrous within boarding distance of the blackship, and boarding planks dropped into place. It was then I got a good look at our enemy as they massed to repel us. Their gunwales were lined with corpse-faced warriors, but if they were living or undead, I could not tell. I was soon swept up in the boarding action. We followed Shadowtongue and Bloodbite across the planks and onto the Cryxian ship. The captain carried no weapons, but he burned and smote the enemy with gouts of horrid green flame and blasts of withering heat. The Cryxians fought like demons, and I soon found myself locked in desperate melee with a creature I had only heard rumors of, a trollkin twisted by Cryxian hell magic called a bloodgorger. It came at me with a pair of axes, roaring a challenge. I stooped to pick up a hand cannon dropped by a slain marauder, aimed, and fired. My shot was true, but the bloodgorger seemed wholly unconcerned by the hole I’d put in its throat. I learned a bit of swordplay in the army, and I put it to good use. I dodged my foe’s first cut, parried the second, and then brought my cleaver down as hard as I could on the brute’s skull. Bone cracked, blood spewed, and my enemy dropped dead at my feet.

name: Name
body:
I had no time to celebrate my victory as the combat whirled around me. Our trolls had joined the fray, and I watched the squid-headed great old one crush the skull of an Cryxian sailor with its mighty claw, splashing crimson gore across the decks and telling me that at least some of our foe were made of normal flesh and bone.
I dragged an injured crewman to safety and sent walking wounded back to our own vessel, all the while fighting as best I could to protect myself and those in my care. We were winning, but whatever future Shadowtongue had seen in that bird’s entrails, he hadn’t seen all of it.
From the hold, green flame and black smoke poured, followed by the horrid forms of half a dozen spider-like helljacks. Worse yet, two figures accompanied this ghoulish assembly. One looked to be human and unspoiled. He was tall, muscular, wore a horned helm, and clutched a vile-looking harpoon in one hand and a curved, butchering blade in the other. His necromechanikal armor marked him as a warcaster, possibly the captain of the blackship.

name: Name
body:
Next to him stood a figure armored head to toe in vicious-looking plate armor. She, too, bore the green fire and smoke-belching stacks of a warcaster. Despite her bone-white pallor, she appeared to be a living creature. She stood unflinching as our crew unloaded hand cannons and deck guns into her ship, a smirk on her face, as if we were no more than insects to be swatted away. A long blade jutted from her right vambrace, but I knew without doubt she could do far worse to a body than just kill it.
First Mate Bloodbite was closest to the enemy ship’s hold, and, Dhunia bless his courage, he charged the blackship’s captain, swinging the anchor he wielded like a great mace. He held his own for a moment, parrying blade and harpoon with more luck than skill, but he was overmatched. The warcaster ducked a wide sweeping blow then rammed his harpoon clean through Bloodbite’s belly. As our first mate sagged to the deck, the warcaster removed his head with a contemptuous swipe of his off-hand blade.

name: Name
body: I looked away, hoping for some signs we could still win this battle. Captain Shadowtongue had engaged the other warcaster and was driving her back with bursts of green fire. A helljack with great tusks and scything claws joined its mistress, and Shadowtongue sent a pair of reef trolls to hold the machine at bay. I dragged more injured back to our ship, watching helplessly as more of our crew fell to the enemy. "Return to The Tenebrous," Shadowtongue shouted and set himself between our fleeing crew and the two Cryxian warcasters. He summoned the great old one to fight by his side, and with that mighty beast and his own fell magic, he fought the two warcasters to a brief stalemate, long enough for us to retreat. Then the blackship’s captain plunged his harpoon into Shadowtongue’s side, and I thought for an instant we would lose him. But our starboard battery opened up again, and the Great Mother must have been looking over us, for one of the cannon balls splintered the blackship’s mast. When it fell, the two warcasters were forced to dive for cover while Shadowtongue limped back to The Tenebrous.

name: Name
body: We drifted away into the fog, bleeding and haunted. Donard 10th The butcher’s bill for our fight with the blackship is twenty dead and fourteen wounded, including the captain himself. Two more will soon join the dead. Their injuries have mortified in a way that defies even trollkin hardiness. I’ve kept them well plied with rum to ease their passing. I saw to the captain’s injury soon after we escaped. I applied healing unguents and stitched him up as he sat silently in his cabin. I likely should have held my tongue, but we’d lost so many, and I needed to know why. "You knew that ship was out there," I said. "Yet you let us attack it anyway. Why?" I don’t know what to expect. Maybe he would rage at me or blast my flesh from my bones with some evil spell. Instead, he shook his head and sighed. "I knew yes, but though I can see glimpses of possible futures, The Tenebrous clouds my sight." He looked me in the eye, and I saw there the mingled fires of rage and grief. "I did not know Captain Aiakos and the other were aboard that ship. I swear to you."

name: Name
body: "Then those we fought and died for nothing," I said. "No, not nothing," Shadowtongue said. "We saw something we were not meant to see. The other warcaster. The darkness in her soul all but smothered me, and her purpose here threatens all of western Immoren. There is value in this knowledge." Fear and grief emboldened me. "Value? What value? We left two score dead on the deck of that blackship, and now their souls will not return to Dhunia. They’ll be . . . they’ll be devoured by some Cryxian abomination." Shadowtongue’s eyes took on a haunted look, and he shook his head. "No. The Tenebrous fed well, the toll is paid, and our comrades remain by our side." Donard 14th We sail south, back to friendlier waters. As I thought, we lost two of the crew injured by the Cryxians. The rest have made a full recovery. Thank Dhunia. We waylaid and plundered a Cygnaran trading ship off Cullenrock Island a few days ago, and the considerable booty brought aboard has raised the crew’s spirits considerably, but my own spirits are lower than ever.

name: Name
body:
You see, I have a nightly visitor. First Mate Bloodbite appears before my bunk every time I lay down to sleep. Tiny pale crabs scuttle from the hole in his belly, and his severed head, which he holds in the crook of his arm, whispers and moans incoherent horrors.
Shadowtongue said those we lost remain by our side, but are they still our comrades? I’ll drink myself to sleep tonight while Bloodbite holds his grim vigil, and I will pray to Dhunia that I won’t soon join him.

name: Brine, Blood, and Bilgewater - Chapter 1 Brine, Blood, and Bilgewater
